content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends treating uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria with Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT). This review evaluates the relative benefits and risks of different ACTs and other treatment combinations to guide malaria control programs. To conduct this review, randomized head-to-head trials of ACTs for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria were analyzed. The ACTs included in the review were dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, artesunate plus mefloquine, artemether-lumefantrine (six doses), artesunate plus amodiaquine, and artesunate plus sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine. Additionally, the non-ACT combination of amodiaquine plus sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine was included for comparison. The primary outcomes were assessed according to the WHO protocol for evaluating antimalarial drug efficacy, and secondary outcomes included effects on P. vivax, gametocyte carriage, hemoglobin levels, and adverse events. The review included 50 studies that met the inclusion criteria. All five ACTs demonstrated polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-adjusted treatment failure rates of less than 10% at most study sites, which aligns with WHO recommendations. Among the ACTs, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine showed superior efficacy compared to other commonly used ACTs. Specifically, in Asia, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine had a lower PCR-adjusted treatment failure rate compared to artesunate plus mefloquine (risk ratio [RR] 0.39, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.19 to 0.79, based on three trials with 1,062 participants). Similarly, in Africa, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine outperformed artemether-lumefantrine (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.64, based on three trials with 1,136 participants). ACTs were also found to be more effective than the non-ACT combination of amodiaquine plus sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine in East Africa. For example, artemether-lumefantrine had a significantly lower PCR-adjusted treatment failure rate compared to amodiaquine plus sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (RR 0.12, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.24, based on two trials with 618 participants). Similarly, artesunate plus amodiaquine was more effective than amodiaquine plus sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.89, based on three trials with 1,515 participants). In terms of reducing the incidence of P. vivax over a 42-day follow-up period, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.43, based on four trials with 1,442 participants) and artesunate plus mefloquine (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.41, based on four trials with 1,003 participants) were more effective than artemether-lumefantrine. The authors concluded that dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine is an effective first-line treatment for P. falciparum malaria. However, the non-ACT combination of amodiaquine plus sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine does not meet WHO recommendations for first-line therapy in certain regions of Africa. In areas where primaquine is not used for the radical cure of P. vivax, ACTs with longer half-lives may offer additional benefits.
